body:
Why the decision was delayed

In 1947, the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir was ruled by Maharaja Hari Singh. The state had a Muslim-majority population and a Hindu ruler. It occupied a strategically important position adjoining the territories of the newly created India and Pakistan.

At Independence, Hari Singh did not immediately accede to either Dominion. The state's political future therefore remained unsettled while most other princely states were establishing formal relationships with India or Pakistan.

The armed incursion and request for help

In October 1947, armed tribal raiders entered Jammu and Kashmir from the direction of Pakistan. Fighting threatened the state's administration and the security of Srinagar. Maharaja Hari Singh requested military assistance from India.

The Government of India required a formal constitutional basis for sending its armed forces to defend the princely state. This led to the execution of an Instrument of Accession.

Two dates that must be distinguished

Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession on 26 October 1947. The Instrument was accepted by Governor-General Lord Mountbatten on 27 October 1947.

Following acceptance, Indian forces were sent to assist in defending the state. The accession established Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional relationship with the Dominion of India while the armed conflict continued.

26 October 1947: Instrument signed by Maharaja Hari Singh.
27 October 1947: Instrument accepted by Lord Mountbatten.

Accession and the territorial conflict were separate questions

Jammu and Kashmir's accession did not immediately end the fighting. India raised the dispute at the United Nations in January 1948. A ceasefire came into effect on 1 January 1949, while the territorial dispute remained unresolved.

It is important to distinguish the legal act of accession from the subsequent armed conflict and competing territorial claims. The former was the ruler's formal decision, accepted by the Governor-General; the latter concerned events that continued after accession.

The contrast with Junagadh is also useful. Junagadh's ruler chose Pakistan before India assumed administration and later conducted a plebiscite. Jammu and Kashmir's ruler signed an Instrument of Accession to India during an armed emergency. Junagadh's February 1948 plebiscite should not be confused with the process followed in Jammu and Kashmir.

Prelims focus

  • Maharaja Hari Singh: Ruler of Jammu and Kashmir in 1947.
  • October 1947: Armed raiders entered the state from the direction of Pakistan.
  • 26 October 1947: Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession.
  • 27 October 1947: Lord Mountbatten accepted it.
  • January 1948: India brought the dispute before the United Nations.
  • Trap: The date of signing was 26 October; the date of acceptance was 27 October.

[GCERT, Class 8, Social Science, Gujarati edition, Chapter 8, India: Post Independence, section on Kashmir; Government of India, Instrument of Accession of Jammu and Kashmir State, dated 26 October 1947, and Governor-General's acceptance dated 27 October 1947; Supreme Court of India, In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution, judgment dated 11 December 2023, historical account of accession, paragraphs 235–237, online text consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Indian soldiers disembark from a transport aircraft as ground personnel unload supplies at Srinagar airfield in October 1947.
pictures.caption: The October 1947 emergency linked Jammu and Kashmir's accession with its request for military assistance.

pictures.alt: Timeline separates the October 1947 emergency, signing on 26 October, acceptance on 27 October, and the later UN referral and ceasefire.
pictures.caption: The ruler's signature and the Governor-General's acceptance occurred on different dates.

title: Jammu and Kashmir: Accession During the 1947 Conflict

body:
Why Kathiawar required administrative consolidation

The Kathiawar peninsula, also known as the Saurashtra region, contained numerous princely states, estates and smaller jurisdictions before Independence. Many of these territories were scattered rather than forming compact administrative units.

NCERT Class 12 records that the region had 14 large states, 119 smaller states and numerous other administrations. The Government of India's 1950 White Paper describes the proposed consolidation as covering 222 states and estates, with further fragmentation within several territories.

These figures describe different categories of political units and should not be added together as though they represented a single uniform count. Their common significance is the extraordinary fragmentation of authority in Kathiawar.

Separate administrations could make roads, revenue collection, courts and public services difficult to coordinate. Merely obtaining Instruments of Accession from individual rulers would not remove every such difficulty. A common regional government was therefore needed.

The creation of a United State

Several Kathiawar rulers agreed to combine their territories through a formal covenant, meaning a binding agreement to establish a common political organisation.

The covenant was signed on 23 January 1948. The resulting United State of Kathiawar, later known as the United State of Saurashtra, was inaugurated by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel on 15 February 1948.

The union established a common executive, legislature and judiciary. Instead of each participating principality maintaining a completely separate governing structure, the new state could administer its combined territory through shared institutions.

Important rulers and institutions

Maharaja Krishnakumarsinhji of Bhavnagar supported the transition to responsible government, in which ministers become answerable to representatives rather than exercising authority solely at the ruler's discretion. Bhavnagar subsequently became part of the Saurashtra union.

The Jam Saheb of Nawanagar, Digvijaysinhji, served as Rajpramukh, the constitutional head of the union. This office was associated with the new union of princely states; it was distinct from the separate offices previously held by the rulers of individual principalities.

Rajkot was the capital of Saurashtra, and U. N. Dhebar served as its Chief Minister.

Junagadh became part of Saurashtra later

The Saurashtra union was inaugurated in February 1948, but Junagadh's integration into its administration followed later. After the public vote and further political decisions, the Saurashtra government took over Junagadh's administration on 20 January 1949.

This sequence shows that the formation of the regional union and the addition of all its eventual territories were not completed on the same day.

Prelims focus

  • Kathiawar: Historical region corresponding to much of present-day Saurashtra.
  • 23 January 1948: Covenant for the United State of Kathiawar signed.
  • 15 February 1948: United state inaugurated by Sardar Patel.
  • Rajpramukh: Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji of Nawanagar.
  • Capital: Rajkot; Chief Minister: U. N. Dhebar.
  • Trap: Junagadh's administration was transferred to Saurashtra on 20 January 1949, after the union had already been formed.

[NCERT, Class 12, Political Science, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed p. 16; GCERT, Class 8, Social Science, Gujarati edition, Chapter 8, India: Post Independence, section on Bhavnagar and Saurashtra; Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States (1950), Part 5, Formation of Unions: Saurashtra, paragraphs 126–127 and Appendix XXXIV, printed pp. 49–50, and Part 11, paragraph 223, consulted online 22 November 2026; Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: Rajkot, Part A, historical background, printed p. 15.]

pictures.alt: Scattered Kathiawar states formed a union with shared institutions in 1948; NCERT and White Paper counts use different classifications and must not be added.
pictures.caption: Saurashtra transformed many separate states and estates into a common regional administration.

title: Saurashtra: Bringing Kathiawar's Princely States Together

body:
Why Kutch did not join the Saurashtra union in 1948

Kutch, also written Kachchh, was a princely state in western India adjoining the Rann of Kutch. Although it belonged to the wider historical and cultural region that would later form Gujarat, its immediate administrative integration differed from that of neighbouring Saurashtra.

The Government of India considered Kutch's geography, administrative needs and requirements for infrastructure and development. It concluded that direct administration by the central government would be more suitable than incorporating Kutch into the new Saurashtra union.

Consequently, Kutch followed the path of a centrally administered territory, while several Kathiawar states were brought together into a regional union.

The Merger Agreement of 4 May 1948

The Maharao of Kutch, Madansinhji, entered into a Merger Agreement on 4 May 1948 with the Government of India.

Under the agreement, the Maharao transferred full governing authority over the state to the Dominion government. Article 1 specified that the transfer of administration would take effect on 1 June 1948.

The state thereafter came under central administration through a Chief Commissioner, an official administering the territory on behalf of the central government.

Accession and merger must be kept separate

Kutch's political connection with the Dominion of India preceded the merger agreement. Its initial accession established the constitutional relationship with India, while the later merger agreement transferred the actual administration of the state.

Thus, 4 May 1948 was the date of the merger agreement, whereas 1 June 1948 was the effective transfer date specified in that agreement. These dates describe different legal steps.

The relevant date in the signed agreement

Article 1 of the signed Kutch Merger Agreement explicitly states 1 June 1948 as the effective date for transferring administration. That date is supported by the agreement itself and by later judicial discussion of Kutch's administration.

What the Kutch example demonstrates

Integration did not require every princely state to become part of a union of neighbouring princely states. Different solutions were used according to geography, size and administrative circumstances.

In Saurashtra, many rulers agreed to form a common regional state. In Kutch, the ruler ceded governing authority directly to the Government of India. Both arrangements contributed to the territorial consolidation of independent India.

Prelims focus

  • Kutch or Kachchh: Former princely state integrated through direct central administration.
  • Maharao Madansinhji: Ruler who signed the merger agreement.
  • 4 May 1948: Kutch Merger Agreement signed.
  • 1 June 1948: Effective date for transfer of administration under Article 1.
  • Chief Commissioner: Official through whom central administration was exercised.
  • Trap: Kutch was not part of the United State of Saurashtra in 1948.

[Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States (1950), Part 5, Centrally Merged States: Kutch, paragraph 118 and Appendix XXIX, Kutch Merger Agreement, especially Article 1, signed 4 May 1948, online transcription consulted 22 November 2026; Supreme Court of India, judgment reported in Supreme Court Reports, 1957, volume 1, printed p. 747 and following, historical account of Kutch's transfer of administration.]

pictures.alt: Saurashtra formed a regional union; Kutch came under central administration through a Chief Commissioner. Both became parts of the Indian Union.
pictures.caption: Kutch's central merger and Saurashtra's regional union were different administrative arrangements.

title: Kutch: A Separate Route to Integration with India

body:
Integration involved more than joining the Union

The successful integration of princely states occurred through several related but distinct changes. A ruler's accession established a constitutional connection with the Indian Dominion. A later merger agreement could transfer the state's government to another authority. A union covenant could combine several princely states into one larger administrative unit.

These arrangements helped replace numerous separate systems of administration with more coordinated governing institutions. Over time, territories that had once been ruled by hereditary princes became parts of the constitutional structure of independent India.

Different kinds of administrative units in 1950

When the Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950, the country initially had different categories of states and territories.

  • Part A states: Generally former Governor's provinces of British India.
  • Part B states: Mainly former princely states or unions of princely states. Saurashtra was a Part B state.
  • Part C states: Included certain centrally administered territories and former Chief Commissioner's provinces. Kutch was a Part C state.
  • Part D territory: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

These were historical constitutional categories. They explain how territories were organised at the commencement of the Constitution; they should not be confused with the later division into states and Union territories.

Saurashtra and Kutch in 1950

Saurashtra was a Part B state. Kutch was a Part C state. Both belonged to India, but their initial administrative arrangements were different.

Reorganisation in 1956

The creation of larger administrative units did not end the question of state boundaries. During the early years after Independence, demands grew for states whose boundaries better reflected regional languages and administrative needs.

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganised much of the country with effect from 1 November 1956. Under this reorganisation, the separate states of Saurashtra and Kutch were incorporated into the enlarged, bilingual Bombay State, which contained substantial Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking areas.

At the same time, the earlier constitutional categories of Part A, Part B and Part C states were abolished as part of the new arrangements for states and Union territories.

The formation of Gujarat in 1960

The bilingual Bombay State did not remain a permanent solution. Demands for separate Gujarati-speaking and Marathi-speaking states continued.

Parliament enacted the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, which received assent on 25 April 1960. Under Section 3, the new State of Gujarat was formed on 1 May 1960, and the remaining Bombay State became the State of Maharashtra.

The territories forming Gujarat included the former Saurashtra region, the former Kutch state and other Gujarati-speaking areas of the earlier Bombay State.

The main differences among the integration cases

The principal princely-state cases illustrate different political and administrative problems:

  • Junagadh: The Nawab chose Pakistan, but administration passed to India and a subsequent plebiscite strongly supported joining India.
  • Hyderabad: The Nizam sought independence; negotiations, internal unrest and Operation Polo preceded integration.
  • Jammu and Kashmir: Maharaja Hari Singh signed an Instrument of Accession during the armed crisis of October 1947.
  • Saurashtra: Numerous princely states and estates were combined through a union covenant.
  • Kutch: Governing authority was transferred directly to the Indian government through a merger agreement.

The common outcome was the extension of the Indian Union's territorial and constitutional framework. The methods differed because the initial political choices, local circumstances and administrative requirements differed.

Prelims focus

  • 26 January 1950: Constitution came into force; Saurashtra was Part B and Kutch was Part C.
  • 1 November 1956: Saurashtra and Kutch became parts of the enlarged Bombay State.
  • Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960: Legal basis for creating Gujarat and Maharashtra.
  • 1 May 1960: Formation of Gujarat State.
  • Section 3: Provision for formation of Gujarat under the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960.
  • Trap: The creation of Saurashtra in 1948 was not the creation of Gujarat State in 1960.

[NCERT, Class 12, Political Science, Politics in India since Independence, Chapter 1, Challenges of Nation Building, printed pp. 16–23; GCERT, Class 9, Social Science, Gujarati edition, Chapter 7, Post-Independence India, sections on state formation and reorganisation; Government of India, Ministry of States, White Paper on Indian States (1950), Part 11, Territorial Integration, paragraph 224, online transcription consulted 22 November 2026; Census of India 1961, Gujarat, General Population Tables, Part II-A, section on jurisdictional changes and reorganisation in 1956; Government of India, Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, Act 11 of 1960, Sections 2–3, India Code text consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Saurashtra and Kutch became Part B and Part C states, joined Bombay State on 1 November 1956, then became part of Gujarat on 1 May 1960.
pictures.caption: Saurashtra and Kutch followed different early paths before becoming parts of Bombay State and then Gujarat.

pictures.alt: Five princely-state cases pair distinct integration methods with their circumstances and dated milestones.
pictures.caption: The principal cases demonstrate different routes to political and administrative integration.

title: Administrative Consolidation and the Formation of Modern Gujarat
